THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI KAMAL 
NATH): (a) India has not yet signe d any Free Trade Agreement with

The list of items under the Early Harvest Scheme has been finalised after 
consultations with the administrative Ministries/Departments and the domestic 
stakeholders. The tariff preferences would be available only for those products 
which enjoy the 'originating status' as prescribed under the Rules of Origin 
which are-integral part of the Free Trade Agreement. The Agreement also provides 
for trade defence measures which an importing country can take recourse to. In case 
of a surge in imports and injury to the domestic industry, a country is allowed 
to take measures such as anti-dumping and safeguards.

THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL): (a) to 
(c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
As per the existing scheme of financing Relief Expenditure, the State 
Government concerned is responsible for undertaking relief and rehabilitation 
measures in the areas affected by natural calamities, including floods out

of the corups of the Calamity Relief Fund (CRF), which is contributed by the 
Government of India and the State Government in the ratio of 3:1. The State of 
Madhya Pradesh has been allocated an amount of Rs. 254.23 crore in the CRF for 
the year 2005-06, comprising Rs. 190.67 crore Central contribution and Rs. 
63.56 crore as State contribution. The first instalment of Central Share of CRF 
amounting to the Rs. 95.335 crore has b een released to the State of Madhya 
Pradesh on 6th July, 2005. 
In case the calamity is of a severe nature and the funds available in the 
State's CRF account are not sufficient, additional assistance is provided to the States 
out of the National Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF), after following the 
established procedure. The Government of India supplements the efforts of the 
State Governments by providing financial and logistic support, wherever 
necessary. The financial assistance in the wake of natural calamities is provided as 
per the approved items and norms of expenditure from CRF/NCCF. 
The Government of Madhya Pradesh has submitted its Memorandum 
recently. With regard to th e loss to agriculture in Madhya Pradesh, the State 
Government have in their Memorandum indicated that a west area in the nine 
districts affected by heavy rains and floods still remains to be sown. According 
to the State Government, the expected area under delayed sowing is 7.86 lakh ha. 
area unsown due to floods is 3.86 lakh ha. and area under re-sowing is 0.22 
lakh ha. 
The State Government Memorandum has sought Central assistance of a total 
amount of Rs. 628.21 crore for relief the flood affected persons and for the 
repair and restoration of damaged property/infrastructure in the areas affected 
by floods in July, 2005. An amount of Rs. 23.88 crore has inter-alia been sought 
for providing input subsidy for a cropped area of 2.39 lakh ha. belonging to 
small and marginal farmers. 
An Inter-Ministerial Team has visited the State for assessment of damage 
and requirement of funds for relief operations by the State Government. The 
report of the Team is yet to be received. Action on the report of the Central 
Team is taken by the Government, in consonance with the extant norms of 
assistance and the laid down procedure.

†*151. SHRI KRIPAL PARMAR: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS

for punishment for offences against women. These Sections are (i) section 304 
B(dowry Death) (ii) section 354 (assault or criminal force to women with intent 
to outrage her modesty, (iii) section 376 (Rape); (iv) section 498 (enticing or

police officer and public servant on a woman in custody.

Floods in the country 
*157. SHRI MURLI DEORA: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether floods have caused havoc in many States of the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the amount of loss caused to each State; 
(c) whether Government have provided relief and given grants to overcome the 
situation; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the steps taken to check floods? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI S. REGUPATHY): (a)to(d) During the current South West Monsobn 2005, 
a number of States have been affected by floods causing loss of life and extensive 
damage to property and infrastructure. The provisional estimates of damage 
due to the floods in the current South West Monsoon season, based on the 
assessment reports received from the State Governments, are given in the 
Statement-I (See below). 
As per the existing Scheme of Financing Relief Expenditure, the State 
Government concerned is responsible for undertaking relief and rehabilitation 
measures in the areas affected by natural calamities, including floods out of the 
corpus of the Calamity Relief Fund (CRF), which is contributed by the 
Government of India and the State Government in the ratio of 3:1. The 
Government of India supplements the efforts of the State Governments by 
providing financial and logistic support, wherever necessary. In case the calamity 
is of a servere nature and the funds available in the State's CRF account are not 
sufficient, additional assistance is provi ded to the States out of the National 
Calamity Contingency Fund (NCCF), after following the established procedure. 
The financial assistance in the wake of natural calamities is provided as per 
approved items and norms of expenditure under CRF/NCCF.

funds available in the corpus of the CRF. These measures inter-alia include

the Government in consonance with the extant items and norms of assistance 
and the laid down procedure. 
The Schemes for flood control are planned, funded and executed by the State 
Governments. The role of Central Government is broadly technical and 
promotional in nature. The Government of India have initiated various measures 
for assisting the State in the management of floods. These measures inter-alia 
include: 
(a) The recommendations of the Rashtriya Barh Ayog, which provides the 
framework for the flood management strategy in the country, have been 
forwarded to the State Government for implementation. 
(b) Preparation of comprehensive plans for flood management for all the 23 river 
systems of the river Ganga by the Ganga Flood Control Commission. 
(c) Setting up of Brahamputra Board for flood mangement in Brahamputra and its 
major tributaries. 
(d) Constitution of a Task Force on.flood management/soil erosion to 
examine the problem of floods and erosion in Assam and the neighbouring States 
of West Bengal, Bihar and Eastern Uttar Pradesh.

detailed project report for Sapta Kosi High Dam Multipurpose Project and Sun

Law to protect witnesses 
*158. SHRI S.P.M. SYED KHAN: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in the absence of a law to protect the rights of 
victims/witnesses, in many cases, crucial witnesses turn hostile, making the 
present laws useless; 
(b) whether any committee has recommended enactment of a law giving 
protection to the witnesses; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; and 
(d) whether Government have any proposal to bring forth a Bill to protect 
witnesses' rights? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI S. REGUPATHY): (a) to (d) Though measurs are taken by the 
Investigating agencies/Prosecution to provide protection to witnesses on their 
own or sometimes at the instance of the courts, inadequacies of legal 
provisions in this regard have been noticed. The Law Commission as well as the 
Committee constituted under the Chairmanship of (Dr.) Justice V.S. Malimath to 
consider necessary measures to reform  the Criminal Justice System in the 
country have aiscussed the problem of witnesses turning hos tile and have 
recommended suggestions to address the problem. 
The problem of witness turning hostile is being sought to be tackled 
through suitable amendments in the Indian Penal Code and the Criminal 
Procedure Code, 1973 vide the Criminal Law (Amendment) Bill 2003. The 
relevant provisions of the Bill in this regard are as under:— 
(a) insertion of a new section 195A in IPC to provide for punishment for 
threatening or inducing any person to give false evidence. 
(b) amendment to section 162 of Cr. PC providing that the statement made 
by a person to a Police Officer, if reduced to writing should be signed by the 
person making it and a copy of .the same should be given to the person signing it. 
52 

[3 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) insertion of a new section 164 A in Cr. PC to make it mandatory for 
recording of evidence of material witness(es) by Magistrate in an offence 
punishable with death or imprisonment for 07 years or more.

(c) whether these sanitary and phytosanitary standards are in line with WTO 
agreements, if so, the details of such provisions and do we comply with such 
standards; and 
(d) what steps are being taken to safeguard country's farm-exports from 
such non-tariff barriers? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) Yes, Sir. Instances of use of 
non-tariff barriers (NTBs), especially in the form of Sanitary and 
Phytosanitary (SPS) standards, on India's farm export by some countries have 
been noticed during the past few years. 
60 

[3 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) A number of instances of adoption or imposition of standards or 
measures on farm exports has been reported. If measures are based on 
evidence of science, and are not being used in an arbitrary and discriminatory 
manner, they are deemed to be compatible with the WTO provisions. 
In case the exporters find that the imposed or adopted standards or 
measures are not based on evidence of science, and are being used in an arbitrary 
and discriminatory manner which is hurting their trade, they inform this Ministry 
either individually or through the export promotion councils, and the matter is 
suitably taken up at the bilateral level with the country concerned or in the SPS 
Committee of the WTO. 
(c) The SPS Agreement encourages Memb ers to base their SPS measures 
on international standards, guidelines and recommendations as developed by the 
Codex Alimentarius Commission (Codex), International Plant Protection 
Convention (IPPC), and the International Office of Epizootics (OIE). It also 
allows Members to introduce or maintain SPS measures which result in a 
higher level of SPS protection than would be achieved by measures based on 
the relevant international standards, guidelines or recommendations if there is 
a scientific justification. India strives to comply with the provisions of the SPS 
Agreement. 
(d) To protect country's farm exports from such non-tariff barriers, a 
number of steps have been initiated which, inter alia, including holding 
bilateral and joint commission meetings, effective participation in the SPS 
Committee meetings, improving sanitary and phytosanitary conditions of 
country's overall exports by establishing and strengthening of certification 
agencies like Export Inspection Council (EIC), capacity and awareness 
building of concerned exporters through trainings, seminars, introducing 
compulsory testing regimes for ce rtain specified commodities before 
shipping and giving financial assistance for quality testing of certain specified 
exportable produces.

New subjects in protocol of WTO 
963. SHRI S. M. LALJAN BASHA:  Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that WTO is including new subjects and 
new areas without proper approval from Member-countries like India; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the WT O has included new subjects like 
'Competition Policy', Labour standards, et c., which were not in the original 
protocols of WTO; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that Gove rnment has not lodged any formal 
protest with WTO; 
 
(d) if so, the reasons for Government not raising this issue in the proper 
fora; and 
(e) the steps proposed in this regard by Government? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) to (e) Decision making in 
World Trade Organisation (WTO) is governed by Article IX of the Marrakesh 
Agreement establishing the WTO. However, decisions in WTO are taken by 
consensus among the WTO Members. Hence, the question of WTO taking any 
decision on inclusion of new subjects and new areas without approval of WTO 
Members does not arise. 
At the Singapore Ministerial Conference of the WTO held in December, 1996, 
it was agreed to set up Working Groups on four issues, namely, 
67 

RAJYA SABHA [3 August, 2005] 
(i) relationship between Trade and Invest ment; (ii) interaction between Trade 
and Competition Policy; (iii) Transparency in Government Procurement and 
(iv) Trade Facilitation. These issues have come to be known as Singapore 
Issues. 
In its Decision of 1 August, 2004 adopting the Framework Agreement 
providing a road map for continuing negotiations under the Doha Work 
Programme up to the Sixth Ministerial Conference of the WTO in Hong Kong, 
China in December, 2005, the WTO General Council, interalia, decided to 
remove the three Singapore issues mentioned at (i) to (iii) above from the 
Doha Work Programme. It decided to commence negotiations on the remaining 
Singapore issue, namely, Trade Facilitation. The concerns and reservations raised 
by developing countries in  starting negotiations on Trade Facilitation have 
largely been met in the modalities agreed for negotiation through extensive 
provision of Special and Differential Treatment for developing countries 
including the least developed countries. The negotiations would also aim at 
having effective provisions of cooperation between customs authorities on trade 
facilitation ana customs compliance issues. 
The Singapore Ministerial Declaration, inter alia, recognised that the 
International Labour Organisation (ILO) is the competent body to set and deal 
with the core labour standards. It re jected the use of labour standards for 
protectionist purposes, and agreed that the comparative advantage of countries, 
particularly, low-wage developing countries, must in no way be put into 
question. The subsequent Ministerial Conference at Doha also reiterated this 
decision. Hence, the issue of core labour standards is within the domain of the 
ILO and not with the WTO.

Issues to be raised by India in WTO conference at Hong Kong 
974. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SI RIGIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) what are the preparations made by Government and what are the 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
80 

[3 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
issues on which India is going to emphasise in the forthcoming Ministerial 
Conference of WTO at Hong Kong; 
(b) whether there is a possibility of  taking up these issues, apart from 
agriculture in the Ministerial meeting; 
(c) if so, what are the possible issues that are going to be discussed; 
(d) whether any consultations have been held with experts in connection with 
agriculture related aspects which are going to be placed before the Ministerial 
meeting; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) to (c) Government maintain an 
active dialogue with various stakeholders to develop India's positions on issues 
under negotiations at the WTO. To achieve our negotiating objectives, India 
has been making concerted efforts to develop common positions with other WTO 
members sharing similar concerns and interests. 
The Sixth Ministerial Conference of the WTO scheduled to be held in Hong 
Kong, China from 13-18 December 2005 would, among other things, review the 
progress of ongoing negotiations launched under the Doha Work Programme and 
take appropriate decisions. The Doha Work Programme covers mainly 
negotiations in Agriculture, Services, Non-Agricultural Market Access (NAMA), 
WTO Rules, Trade & Environment, Trade Facilitation and Development 
Issues. 
The formal agenda of the Ministerial Conference at Hong Kong China 
remains to be finalized. However, it has been proposed by the Chairman of the 
WTO Trade Negotiations Committee that the Conference should aim to achieve 
substantial breakthrough on modalities in Agriculture and Non-Agriculturai 
Market Access (NAMA), a critical mass of  market opening offers in services, 
substantial progress in Rules and Trade Facilitation and a proper reflection of 
development dimension in the negotiations. 
India's approach and priorities in the Doha Work Programme are dictated by its 
national interest. In the agriculture negotiations, the concerns of the large Indian 
farming community remain paramount, particularly their food and livelihood 
security concerns and rural development needs, as also our objective of achieving 
effective market access in goods and services of our 
81 

RAJYA SABHA [3 August, 2005] 
export interests, addressing non-tariff barriers that impede our market access, and fully 
realizing the development dimension in the negotiations. 
(d) to (e) Negotiating objectives in agriculture, and strategies to achieve them, have been 
developed based on analytical work by research institutions such as the National 
Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER), Indian Institute of Foreign Trade (IIFT) 
and the Centre for WTO Studies. An Expert Group on Agriculture consisting of 
eminent agro-economists has been meeting from time to time to provide guidance in the 
agriculture negotiations. Consultations are also held with Governments of States and Union 
Territories at officials and/or Ministerial levels. These processes are intensified depending 
on the exigencies of WTO negotiations. The Government also works closely with other like-
minded countries to build issue based coalitions, such as the G-20 on Agriculture and 
the G-33 on Special Products and Special Safeguard Mechanism.

983. SHRI TARIQ ANWAR: W ill the Minister of COMMERCE AND

imports; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether there will be loss of hundreds of million of dollars of foreign trade 
earnings, if the ban is imposed; and 
(d) if so, the steps taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) Yes, Sir. In September, 
2004, white addressing the inaugural Session of "India-Bangladesh Dialogue 
88 

[3 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
on Young Journalists", organised by the Bangladesh Enterprise Institute (BEI) in 
Dhaka, the Bangladesh Foreign Minister said that "if Dhaka wanted establishing a 
win-win situation, we can end India's US$ 3 billion trade by issuing a Statutory 
Regulatory Order (SRO) on all Indian goods entering Bangladesh". However, 
Bangladesh Government has not formally or informally conveyed any 
imposition of ban on imports from India, nevertheless, it has imposed several 
restrictions on import of Indian goods into Bangladesh. Some of the restrictions 
are as follows:— 
a. Measures restricting import of yarn through landports—From 
9.3.2002, Bangladesh has banned import of yarn through land ports 
from India with an objective of protecting local spinning mills and 
check smuggling. This has forced Indian exporters to export via sea 
route or by air which not only adds to the cost but, more importantly, 
has taken away the lead time advant age that India has been enjoying 
over the years. In addition, Bangladesh offers 15% subsidy to the 
exporters of knitted apparel who use locally spun cotton yarn, thereby 
making foreign origin yarn uncompetitive. 
b. Ban on import of sugar through land ports—Bangladesh has 
imposed ban on import of sugar through all lend ports. We have 
requested the Bangladesh side to relax the ban at least for sugar 
exports by public sector undertakings of the Central/State 
Governments in India. 
c. Ban on import of Indian parent stock chicks into Bangladesh— 
Bangladesh has imposed a ban on parent chicks from India, along with 
some other Asian countries, ostensibly to avert an outbreak of avian flu in 
Bangladesh, despite the fact that India has been declared free from this virus 
by international agencies such as OIE and WHO. The ban has been imposed 
on the basis of tendentious local media reports inspired by vested 
interests. 
d. Mandatory testing requirements—It has come to the High 
Commission's notice that Bangladesh custom authorities have been 
insisting on testing of fresh fruits such as oranges for radioactivity 
content. Due to this requirement, the fresh fruit exporters of North 
Eastern States of India are considerably harassed since they have 
to send the samples to Kolkata for testing. 
e. Khamarbari Certificate—In addition, Bangladeshi importers of Indian 
potato have to obtain Khamarbari Certificate from Bangladesh

authorities. Indian exporters have complained that Bangladesh 
authorities are not even accepting the applications for certification.

Ahluwalia Committee Report on IAF accidents 
1001. SHRI DARA SINGH: Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether an Expert Committee, headed by Air Marshal Ahluwalia, 
set up in December, 2004 to identify causes of accidents in IAF, has 
submitted its report to Government; 
(b) if so, what are the findings/r ecommendations made by the Committee 
in respect of MIG-21 which constitutes 70 percent of the lAF's total fleet; 
(c) whether it is a fact that Pilot error is the cause of 50 per cent of the lAF's accidents, 
a bigger killer than technical defects; and 
(d) if so, the details of suggestions the Committee has made towards 
training of Pilots besides other deficiencies in design or equipment? 
104 

[3 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE): (a) to (d) 
The Expert Committee on Ai rcraft Accidents has submitted its reports to the 
Government in May, 2005. The Committee, based on the analysis of trends, has 
found that older technology aircraft including MiG-21 are more prone to 
failure. The new technology aircraft incorporates improved design features, 
which provides better air safety. 
Pilot error constitutes approximately 43% of the aircraft accidents in the 
Indian Air Force (IAF). The trend is found in all aviation organizations (civil and 
military) across the world. Aircraft acci dents due to Technical Defects (TD) 
accidents account for 39% of the accidents in the IAF. 
The Committee has made wide-ranging recommendations towards 
improving pilot training, covering all aspect of pilot selection and training. These 
include upgrading of selection requirem ent, induction of new "Computerised 
Pilot Selection System" at Air Force Selection Boards, simulator training 
flying, focused training, closer monitoring of the pilots by supervisors, re-
streaming/re-training of pilots, etc.  The Committee has also suggested to 
formulate a strategy to manage the risk inherent in the old technology aircraft, 
monitoring of failure trends and strengthening of quality assurance and 
airworthiness certification procedues at the overhauling facilities of the Indian 
Air Force (IAF) and Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL). 
Necessary flight safety measures, on the basis of recommendations of such 
Committees, are continuously undertaken by the Government.

(c) to (f) There is a well established mechanism for disaster management in place,

Secretary coordinates the relief and rehabilitation measures in the wake of 
natural calamities. 
An officer designated as Relief Commissioner, is responsible in the State to 
ensure all required measures are undertaken any disaster situation, as per the 
provisions contained in the State Reli ef Manual. The Relief Manual provides 
details of various steps required to be taken for response and relief in the event of 
natural disasters. 
The basic responsibility for undertaking rescue, relief and rehabilitation 
measures in the event of a natural disaster is that of the concerned State 
Governments. There measures inter alia include evacuation and shifting of the 
people to the safer places, setting up of relief camps, air dropping of the food 
packets in the marooned areas, providing gratuitous relief, distribution of 
essential commodities, provision of safe drinking water, ensuring adequate 
health and hygiene measures etc. 
In case of a natural disaster of severe nature, the Government of India 
supplements the efforts of the State'Governments by providing financial and 
logistic support. 
The Centre and the affected States have jointly provided a co-ordinated and 
prompt response to the flood situation in various parts of the country. 
In order to strengthen the existing institutional and coordination 
mechanism, a Central legislation is proposed to be enacted. The Disaster 
Management Bill 2005 was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 11 th May 2005. 
The Bill inter alia provides for constitution of Disaster Management Authorities 
at National, State and District levels, formulation and implementation of 
Disaster Management Plans, establishment of National Disaster Response Force 
and Strengthening of National Institute of Disaster Management. These measures 
will facilitate holistic, coordinated and prompt response to any disaster 
situation.

Statement 
Rules relating to captive power plants 
3. Requirements of Captive Generating Plant.— 
(1)    No power plant shall qualify as a 'captive generating plant' under section 
9 read with clause (8) of section 2 of the Act unless— 
(a)    in case of a power plant— 
154 

[3 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(i) not less than twenty six per cent of the ownership is held by the 
captive user(s); and 
(ii) not less than fifty one percent of the aggregate electricity generated in such 
plant, determined on an annual basis, is consumed for the captive 
use: 
Provided that in case of power plant set up by registered cooperative society, 
the conditions mentioned under paragraphs at (i) and (ii) above shall be 
satisfied collectively by the members of the cooperative society:— 
Provided further that in case of association of persons, the captive user(s) 
shall hold not less than twenty six per cent of the ownership . of the plant in 
aggregate ad such captive user(s) shall consume not less than fifty one 
per cent of the electricity generated, determined on an annual basis, in 
proportion to their shares in ownership of the power plant within a 
variation not exceeding ten per cent; 
(b) in case of a generating station ow ned by a company formed as special 
purpose vehicle for such generating station, a unit or units of such generating 
station identified for captive use and not the entire generating station satisfy (s) 
the conditions contained in paragraphs (i) and (ii) of subclause (a) above 
including— 
Explanation:— 
(1) The electricity required to be consumed by captive users shall be 
determined with reference to such generating unit or units in 
aggregate identified for captive use and not with reference to 
generating station as a whole; and 
(2) the equity shares to be held by the captive user (s) in the generating station 
shall not be less than twenty six per cent of the proportionate of the 
equity of the company related to the generating unit or units identified as 
the captive generating plant. 
Illustration:— In a generating station with two units of 50 MW each 
namely Units A and B, one unit of 50 MW namely Unit A may be identified as 
the Captive Generating Plant. The captive users shall hold not less 
155 

RAJYA SABHA [3 August, 2005] 
than thirteen per cent of the equity sh ares in the company (being the twenty 
six per cent proportionate to Unit A of 50 MW) and not less than fifty one per 
cent of the electricity generated in Unit A determined on an annual basis is to 
be consumed by the captive users. 
(2) It shall be the obligation of the captive users to ensure that the 
consumption by the Captive Users at the percentages mentioned in subclauses (a) 
and (b) of sub-rule (1) above is maintained and in case the minimum 
percentage of captive use is not complied with in any year, the entire electricity 
generated shall be treated as if it is a supply of electricity by a generating 
company. 
Explanation.— (1) For the purpose of this rule — 
a. "Annual Basis" shall be determined based on a financial year; 
b. "Captive User" shall mean the end user of the electricity 
generated in a Captive Generating Plant and the term "Captive 
Use" shall be construed accordingly; 
c. "Ownership" in relation to a generating station or power plant 
set up by a company or any other body corporate shall mean the 
equity share capital with voting rights. In other cases ownership 
shall mean proprietary interest and control over the generating 
station or power plant; 
d. "Special Purpose Vehicle" shall mean a legal entity owning, 
operating and maintaining a generating station and with no other 
business or activity to be engaged in by the legal entity.

(b) and (c) The Government is awar e of the study undertaken in the 
identified backward Districts of Yavatmal, Hingoli and Nanded of 
Maharashtra. The major issues raised by the study were (i) non-payment of full 
wages to the target group, (ii) no earmarking of women and no facilities for 
them at the work site, (iii) no transparency being maintained, (iv) non-adherence 
of Guidelines with regards to setting up of local monitoring committees, time bound 
payment of wages to the workers etc. and (v) low piece rate of payment of 
wages. These issues were examined in detail and report of the State Government 
of Maharashtra was also obtained in this regard. The study is based on some 
solitary incidents and most of the issues raised are basically due to provisions of 
the Programme Guidelines not being very clear to the study team and some 
initial implementation related problems being faced by the 
implementing/executing agencies. Detailed para-wise comments of the Ministry 
and the State Government of Maharashtra as well on the issues raised oy the 
study was sent to the leader of the study team, instructions have been 
reiterated to the State Governments to ensure compliance of the Guidelines. 
Moreover, considering the magnitude of the programme that was launched only 
about seven months ago, structures and processes envisaged for creating 
accountability for delivering the benefits intended in the programme may take 
some time to become effective and this itself will need constant, vigilant support 
from all quarters at every level.

Monitoring of implementation of NFFWP 
1091. SHRI URKHAO GWRA BRAHMA: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Ministry takes stock of the progress of implementation of the 
National Food for Work Programme (NFFWP); 
(b) if so, details thereof; 
(c) whether any such mechanism have been developed to monitor the works 
at the ground level so that quality can be ensured; and 
(d) if so, the detail thereof? 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [3 August, 2005] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a) and (b) The 
National Food for Work Programme (NFFWP) has inbuilt mechanism for 
constant and vigilant monitoring through participatory approach. The Monthly 
Progress Reports indicating physical and financial progress are required to be 
sent to the Ministry in the prescribed format. The system of reporting progress has 
been made mandatory from Block to District, District to State and State to the 
Centre. Review meetings at nine regional centres were proposed in the first phase 
to monitor the progress of implementation and the preparation of Perspective Plans, 
out of which eight review meetings have been held at Pune, Patna, Bhubneshwar, 
Hyderabad, Raipur, Bhopal, Guwahati and Ranchi. Some of these meetings were 
also attended by Minister of Rural Development, Government of India and 
Members, Planning Commission. Since the inception of the programme 
(November, 2004) till June, 2005 an amount  of Rs. 2780.99 crore have been 
released alongwith 28.26 Lakh tonnes of foodgrains. Out of which 840.75 crore 
has been utilized and 6.04 lakh MTs of foodgrains distributed. As a result, 
1298.67 lakh mandays have been generated through creation of 36,690 economic 
and social assets and 31,232 works under progress. 
(c) and (d) As has been stated above, the programme guidelines provide for 
constitution of work-wise vigilance and monitoring committees having five to 
nine members of the beneficiaries. Representation of SC/ST and women 
members in the vigilance and monitoring committee is must. The committee is 
required to oversee the progress of the works and the report of this committee is to 
be attached with the completion report which should be placed and discussed in 
the meetings of the Gram Sabha. Besides,  there is schedule of inspections for 
various levels of functionaries from State to the Block level. A certain minimum 
number of inspections have to be carried out by these State Government Officials. 
Apart from the above, Senior Officers of this Ministry also undertake sample 
inspection of works under Area Officers Scheme.

DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL):ta)to (c) No report of 
fudging of muster rolls have so far been received by the Ministry. Some 
instances of lesser payment of wages reported in the press were brought to the 
notice of the State Governments concerned. Madhya Pradesh has registered cases

compensating foodgrains component of wages in the form of cash if the 
foodgrains are not available. This has been done to provide unhindered and timely 
payment of full notified minimum wages to. workers. Instructions have been 
reiterated to the State Governments to en sure compliance of the Guidelines as 
regards minimum wages and other issues.

Capability and technology infusion in man-made fibre sector 
1096. SHRI S.P.M. SYED KHAN: W ill the Minister of TEXTILES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India needs to further enhance the capability and 
infuse technology in man-made fibre sector keeping in view the increased 
consumption of man-made fibre in the world market; 
201 

RAJYA SABHA [3 August, 2005] 
(b) whether it is also a fact that India even though a major producer of cotton 
yarn and fabric, the productivity of cotton as measured by yield, has been 
found to be lower than many countries. 
(c) if so, the details of (a) and (b) above; and 
(d) the steps taken by Government to boost textile sector in the context of (a) 
and(b)above? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): (a) 
and (b) Yes, Sir. 
(c) The consumption of man-made fibres in India is estimated at 2166.94 
million kg. in 2004-05, whereas the production of such fibres is 2124.00 
million kg. and the installed capacity in the country is 2518.67 million kg.. 
India produced 1793 million kg. of cotton fabrics in 2003-04, which accounts 
for 14.38% of world production and India is the second largest producer of 
such fabrics in the world. However, due to increase in domestic and world 
demand for Indian man-made fibres, fabric as well as cotton yarn and 
fabrics, there is need for increasin g the production capability of man-made 
fibres as well as cotton fabrics/yarn in the country. 
The productivity of cotton (2004-05) in India is approximately 440 kgs. per 
hectare, which is much lower than the productivity of cotton in many other 
cotton producing countries like China, Pakistan and USA, which have 
productivity levels at 1119, 773 and 958 kgs. per hectare respectively 
during 2004-05 
(d) The Government has been taking a number of steps from time to 
time for accelerated growth of textile  sector as given in the Statement 
enclosed (See below). 
Statement 
Measures taken by the Government for development of the textile sector 
(i) Cotton development and research programmes like Integrated Cotton 
Development Programme (ICDP) have been launched. 
(ii) Bacillus Thuringiensis (BT) cotton has been released commercially w.e.f. 
2002-03 cotton season by Government of India to fight pest resistance 
being faced by cotton farmers in major qualities of the crop. 
202 

[3 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(iii) Promoting integrated cotton cultivation (contract farming) involving 
availability of seeds, pesticides, fertilizers etc. to  the farmers for 
obtaining desired quality of cotton. 
(iv) Setting up of a Cotton Technology Mission in February, 2000 with an 
outlay of Rs. 593 crores to improve the quality of cotton fibre at 
reasonable cost with a view also to export cotton at competitive prices 
in comparison to other exporting countries. 
(v) Launching of Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme w.e.f. 1.4 1999 to 
facilitate modernisation and upgradation of textile sector. 
(vi) The import of a large number of capital goods of man-made fibres/ yarns 
industry has been allowed under concessional customs duty of 5%. Besides 
the cost of machinery has also been reduced through fiscal policy measures. 
Except for mandatory excise duty on man-made filament yarns and man-
made staple fibres, the whole value addition chain has been given an 
excise exemption option. 
(vii) 100% foreign direct investment is allowed in the textile sector under the 
automatic route. 
(viii) The Government has dereserved the readymade garments, hosiery and 
knitwear from the SSI sector. 
(ix) An Apparel Park for Export Scheme has been launched to impart a 
focused thrust for setting up of apparels manufacturing units of 
international standards of potential growth centres and to give fillip to 
exports. Under the Scheme Government gives grants upto Rs. 17 
crores per apparel park for infrastructure work, training and common 
facilities. 
(x) Textile Centres Infrastructure Development Scheme (TCIDS) 
(Centrally sponsored) has been introduced with the objective of 
modernizing infrastructure facilities at major traditional textile centres of the 
country. Government of India gives grant upto Rs. 20 crores for a 
particular centre. 
(xi) In order to facilitate modernisation of the Powerloom Sector, schemes 
such as High-tech Weaving Parks, Modernisation and Strengthening of 
Powerloom Service Centres, Group Workshed Scheme and Credit 
Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme @ 20% have been introduced 
203 

RAJYA SABHA [3 August, 2005] 
(xii) To facilitate import of state-of-the-art machinery to make our products 
internationally competitive in post quota regime, in 2005-06 Budget, the 
customs duty on textile machinery has been brought down to 10% 
except 23 items of machinery appearing in List 49 which attract Basic 
Customs Duty (BCD) of 15%. The concessional duty of 5% continues to 
be at 5% on most of the machinery items. 
(xiii) Government has launched the Debt Restructuring Scheme w.e.f. Sept., 
2003 with the principal objective to permit banks to lend to the textile 
sector at 8-9% rate of interest. 
(xiv) The National Institute of Fashion Technology (NIFT) has been set up to 
provide a leadership role in sensitizing the industry to the concept of 
value addition by inducting trained professionals to manage the 
industry. This has resulted in an increased demand for trained 
professionals in various sectors servicing the industry.

1097. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be 
pleased to state:

industry under the proposed SAFTA; 
(c) whether the Bangladesh garment industry would not be granted 
preferential status for the Indian market; and 
(d) the details of specific clauses that are being incorporated into SAFTA for the 
protection of the Indian textile industry? 
THE MINISTER OF TEXTILES (SHRI SHANKERSINH VAGHELA): (a) to 
(d) There are 429 textiles tariff lines in the preliminary indicative Negative List of 
India. The Negative Lists of South As ian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) member 
countries have not yet been finalized by the Committee of Experts on SAFTA. 
Under the SAFTA Agreement, Bangladesh would get the benefits that are 
available to other contracting members on MFN basis, and besides get other 
such concessions that are extended to Least Developed Countries (LDCs) 
contracting members. 
204 

[3 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Adetailed safeguard mechanism is in place under Article 16 of Agreement on 
SAFTA in case of surge in imports on preferential treatment from SAARC 
countries. Besides, export in textiles (similar to any other sector) under SAFTA 
will be subject to fulfilment of criteria defined in the Rules of Origin under 
Article 18 of Agreement on SAFTA.

SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH (Andhra Pradesh): Thank you, Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, 
forgiving the co-signatory of the original Calling Attention Motion one minute at the fag end 
of this debate. Sir, I am not going to repeat many of the points that have been made in 
the debate by Shri Pramod Mahajan and his colleagues. But, I will just raise three or 
four basic issues for the hon. Home Minister's attention with the hope that the crisis, that we 
have faced and which we will continue to face, will be converted into an opportunity. 
Everytime there is a crisis in this country., threre are many people who try to create 
political mileage and political capital, but there are also those who try to see this as an 
opportunity for improvement, whether it was Gujarat earthquake, tsnami and now the 
latest catastrophe that has overtaken Mumbai and Maharashtra. Sir, when Gujarat earthquake 
tragedy happened, there was a lot of talk on disaster management and a National Disaster 
Management Authority was indeed set up. Then, tsunami occurred. Then, the Government, 
which had changed by then, said that they would set up a National Disaster Management 
Authority; that they would come forward with legislation, and they would create empowered 
authorities at the State level and at the national level and we would be in a better position to 
manage national disasters. Now, Sir, let us use this opportunity, let us use this new crisis 
because I am sure, three months from now, there will be another crisis somewhere in 
some part of the country. We will have a similar debate. We will make same points. We 
will have the same political points-scoring between parties. I think, let us today ensure 
that in this session of Parliament, we will get the disaster management law passed. I 
mean, at least, that is something which we can do, instead of giving advice to the rest of 
the world, what is it that we can do as law makers. In the last session, the Bill was introduced. 
It is now before the Standing Committee. I would request you that let us, as an expression of 
our determination to be better prepared for future disasters, please direct the Chairperson of the 
Standing Committee on Home Affair to expedite the submission of the Report so that before we 
disperse on the 26th of this month-and if need be, let us sit for three days more; let us extend 
this session-let us get this law passed in this session of Parliament. Let us not wait for winter 
session and let us pass it before

first request to you, Sir, and to the ho n. Home Minister to ensure that this

give a concrete expression of our concerns. I am not saying that this law is 
going to solve all problems. But it is one concrete manifestation of the lawmakers' 
resolve to deal with natural disasters in a much more organised and systematic

take a lead in this regard. 
Secondly, Sir, Mr. Mahajan made one point, and, I think, this is the point 
which I also raised last week when we had the debate on flood and the drought 
situation in the country. There has been a complete collapse of the forecasting 
system as far as natural disasters generally, and, the monsoon particularly is 
concerned. I don't have to get into the history of it. We saw this in 2002, we saw 
this in 2003, we saw this in 2004, and, in 2005, we are seeing this. I would 
request, Sir, that we have a full-fledged debate on this issue. In spite of the fact 
that we are the world's fourth largest'economy, in spite of the fact that we are a 
major IT power, major nuclear power, major manufacturing power, Sir, the fact 
of the matter is that we are still dependent on the monsoons, the fact of the matter 
is that 40 per cent of India's cultivated area is rain fed, and, the fact of the matter is 
that 45 per cent of the va riation of economic growth in this country comes on 
account on only the monsoons. If the rains are good, India shines. If the rains 
are bad, we have concerns for the Aam Aadmi. I think, we must recognize that 
we are dependent on the monsoon in more respects than one. We cannot 
predict the monsoon with certainty, Sir, and, let us also not overdo our scientific 
prowess. Nowhere in the world does this happen. It is an extraordinarily 
complex scientific system. But, I think, with today's technology that is available 
to us, with today's skills that are available to us, both in India and abroad, it should 
be possible for us to do better showing than what we have done in the recent past. I 
would request the hon. Home Minister, very senior Member in the Cabinet, that 
we have a debate in the House where the Minister of Science and

Sir, the third issue, which is very important, is the whole issue of municipal administration. I 
know some ideas have been suggested by nominated Members, which created a lot of 
heat in the House, but I do want to say that there is a very serious problem of municipal 
administration. Sir, the last year Budget of the Bombay Municipal Corporation, which Mr. 
Mahajan's party and his allies control, was 7,000 crores of rupees, out of which the capital

Corporation, as much as I am not sure, who would want to blame the State Government 
because we all recognise that this was an unprecedented calamity.

have to repeat. It has a Budget of Rs. 7,000 crores last year, out of which, Rs. 1700

Sir, the August House has alread y been informed that there were 
unprecedented rains in Mumbai and other parts of the Maharashtra since 22nd 
July. Between 26th and 27th July 2005, within a span of 24 hours, T hane, 
Mumbai and Sub-urban areas recorded between 700 mm and 920 mm rainfall, a 
phenomenon of grave magnitude. Due to heavy and unprecedented spells of 
rains, 17 out of 35 districts in Maharashtra have been affected, in which besides 
Mumbai and its sub urban areas, the other-districts affected, were inier-alia 
Thane, Nanded, Raigad, Ratnagari, Sangli, Satara, Kolahapur, Akola, Bhandara 
and Parbhani. 
A total of 1.20 crore population have been affected. The number of villages affected 
are 300.962 persons lost their lives, 122 persons suffered injuries while 66 persons 
are reported to be missing. 52000 persons have been evacuated to safer places. 
A large number of livestock comprising of 1200 buffalos and 15000 sheep and 
goat have perished in these floods. 
There has been extensive damage to infrastructure and communication which 
virtually paralyzed traffic in Mumbai and sub urban Mumbai and other parts of 
the State. The Mumbai-Goa National Highway and Mumbai-Pune express way were 
adversely affected. Railway services on Western, Centra! and Konkan railways 
were severely affected and air services also came to a virtual standstill due to 
heavy rains and poor visibility. The telecommunication network, water and 
power supply were also adversely affected in these flood affected areas. 
The State Government responded to the situation. The primary focus of the 
State Government was to put in place t he basic infrastructure and connectivity. 
As the Hon'ble Members have already been informed that the essential services 
i.e. electricity, water supply, local transport including Railways and Air services 
have been restored to a large extent. The Government of Maharashtra have 
taken various steps to provide the succor 
261 

RAJYA SABHA [3 August, 2005] 
to the affected people. 20 Kg. of foodgrains and 10 litres of Kerosene are being distributed to 
each of the affected families. Presently, the attention of the Government is rivetted on 
garbage disposal which has become a major thrust area of operations. 
During the course of the debate, there have been several valuable suggestions 
made by the Hon'ble Members. I would initially join the members of the House in 
recording the appreciation for the patience and fortitude with which the public of Mumbai 
and other parts of the States have responded to such a grave situation. Some Members have 
expressed concern about the weaker sections including slum dwellers who are the most 
vulnerable in such calamities. To meet their immediate requirements, the State Government 
has started distributing ex gratia assistance to all affected families, @ of Rs.1000 per 
person subject to a maximum of Rs. 5000 per family. The State Government is also 
attending to the need of the small traders and shopkeeper who do not have any insurance 
cover, by providing assistance of Rs. 10,000. The stall holders and handcart pullers will 
also be given assistance of Rs. 5000 and Rs. 2500 respectively. The insurance companies 
have been asked to augment their staff and expeditiously clear all insurance claims. 
Almost all the Members have expressed serious concern over the poor and antiquated 
drainage system and the need to replace and augment the same with a better system. To 
address the problem effectively, the State Government has to adopt a multi-pronged strategy 
wherein the problems of urban congestion, encroachments on riverbanks, nallas and 
water courses would have to be suitably addressed. The Municipal Corporation of Mumbai 
would have to prepare a suitable plan for providing Mumbai and its sub urban area with an 
effective drainage system. I assure the Hon'ble Members that the Government of India would 
render necessary assistance to the State Government in planning and implementing this 
project. The proposal for this project can be suitably handled to get aid from the World Bank 
also. 
Some members have expressed concern over the reliability of the forecasting system 
of the Indian Meteorological Department. I have been informed that the IMD is 
strengthening and upgrading its observational and telecommunication network. IMD is 
reported to be introducing high resolution numerical models for improved temporal and 
spatial weather prediction. The rains that occurred are unusual, forecast done by the

Meteorological organizations, world over have not been able to give accurate information 
about it. 
Hon'ble Members have also expressed their apprehension about the likely outbreak of 
water borne disease and epidemics. In this context it would be pertinent to mention that the 
State Government is assigning due priority to the removal of garbage and carcasses. The State 
Government is also paying due attention to the health needs of the people in the flood 
affected areas. More than 100 teams of doctors and para medics have been deployed in 
Mumbai while 500 teams are being deployed in 16 other flood affected districts. Essential 
medicines are being provided in adequate quantities. The Government of India has yesterday 
airlifted and provided the State Government with 25 MTs of bleaching powder. 50 lakh tablets 
of halogen, 50,000 capsules of doxycycline and 5 lakh tablets of chtoroquine have also been 
provided. The Government of India will continue to provide necessary medical support to the 
State Government to deal effectively with the situation. The State Government has already 
launched a mass awareness campaign so that the people of Mumbai are duly sensitized to 
adopt proper health and hygiene standards. However, the State Government would have to 
exercise due vigilance in the slum areas and jhopad patties. 
As the Members are aware that Government of India has introduced the Disaster 
Management Bill 2005 in this august House on 11th May 2005 to provide for requisite 
institutional mechanism and disaster management plans for a holistic, coordinated and 
prompt response and to prepare plans and projects to deal with disaster situations before 
they occur. The Bill inter-alia provides for setting up of Disaster Management Authorities 
at National, State and District levels, constitution of a National Disaster 
Response Force, Strengthening of National Institute of Disaster Management. 
Considering the severity of-the flood situation in Mumbai and some other affected 
parts of Maharashtra, the Government of India had made an immediate adhoc release of Rs. 
500 crore and 10,000 MT of foodgrains to enable the State Government to provide 
relief. For restoration of infrastructure in  the city of Mumbai and the State, the 
Government of Maharashtra is expected to prepare a comprehensive plan and send it to the 
Government of India for its consideration and adoption, which would be

For the long distance trains coming fr om the Northern, Eastern, Southern 
and South Central parts of the country  alternative terminals having road

I have spoken to the Railway Minister and requested him to expedite the

believe, is a piece of information which should be shared with the country, through this House, 
Sir, as soon as the divers were taken out of their chamber where they were under-going 
decompression, we started towing the MSV Samudra Suraksha to the coast, using Sindhu-
V as the towing vessel. The ship was already listing four or five degrees. But, 
unfortunately, it was not the Samudra Suraksha, but the Sindhu-V whose propeller broke. 
Therefore, we had to send another towing vessel, the Neel Kamal. We also contacted several 
professional salvaging companies. But, all of them said they could not help because the 
weather condition was much too bad. We had also arranged, through the SCI, a repair 
workshop with a portable generator to get going on the Samudra Suraksha, as soon as it 
arrived at the coast. We sent out the Samudrika-I with the requisite materials. But, 
unfortunately, they were not able to board the Samudra Suraksa because of the very, very 
furious weather. Then Sir, we tried to ensure that there would be sheltered water space 
for the Samudra Suraksha. But, then, it was decided that because in a restrict space 
things may go wrong, it would be better to keep it at sea and leave the Neel Kamal to 
provide the manoeuvrability, Another vessel, the Feroze Gandhi, was also sent out. But, 
unfortunately, the weather condition* were far too bad to do the towing, the listing continued 
and it had reached 12 degrees. At that time, the two towing lines, had they beep put, even 
then, we may have succeeded in bringing it to the shore. But, even though the Neel 
Kamal was cruising at an extremely slow speed, it was simply not possible to save the 
vessel and it sank. And with it, we have lost a significant element of forensic evidence. But,

Sir, I have been asked by Shri Mahajan to indicate what might have been in 
a preliminary sense the possible reasons for this accident. In doing so, I would 
like to clarify some misconceptions that have crept in by sections of the media 
rushing to judgement without all the information available. 
Sir, the first point I need to make is that multi-purpose supply vessel, (MSV), 
is not the same thing as an offshore supply vessel (OSV). So, all the standards 
and norms that apply to an OSV, an o ff-shore supply vessel, should not 
automatically be placed on an MSV; an  MSV is a far more sophisticated 
vessel. It does have a dynamic positioning system, which means that the 
thrusters on it work in such a manner as to keep it in a single place during diving 
operations because when these diving operations take place in the open sea, it 
would be dreadful if divers went into water and by the time they started coming, up, 
the vessel have shifted somewhere else. So, the system that they have, the 
automatic system of keeping the thrusters going is used when the MSV is 
stationed at one point on the high seas in order to able to direct and then pull back 
the divers who have to go for undersea operations. But when the MSV is moving 
in, what is called, in navigation mode, then the thrusters are not in auto-mode, 
they are manually operated. When this MSV was coming alongside the 
platform, it was moving, and therefore it was in navigation-mode. And, the 
expectation was that it would be, for a few minutes, alongside the platform and 
having completed that operation, it w ould move off. So, the thrusters were 
operated in a manual-mode at that time. There is absolutely nothing unusual 
about the MSV coming alongwide. There is no provision that it should remain a 
hundred meters away. In fact, one of the chief purposes of an MSV is to be able 
to come alongside, sometimes, for fairly easy operations like getting food and 
nutrition supplied; on others, as in this case, for medical purposes where a 
personnel basket is lowered from the platform towards the sea and somebody who 
is injured is transfered on to the personnel basket and is literally pulled up on to the 
platform; and, this is, in fact, the operation that has taken place? Nor is it true to 
say, as some sections of the media have said, that it should only come to one 
side of the vessel and not the other.

possible external State-mounted attack. So, these
